title: Cornell president says university will examine role of Greek life after rape allegation
description:
Cornell University
As outrage builds around the case involving a Cornell University student allegedly gang-raped in a fraternity house in October 2024, the university’s president has broken his silence with a statement Saturday.
Here’s the latest:
University president speaks out: “This is a defining moment in Cornell’s history,” Cornell’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, said in the video statement calling Jane Doe’s allegations “deeply disturbing.” Kotlikoff said he supports the governor’s decision to turn the criminal investigation over to the New York Attorney General and welcomes an independent review by an outside law firm into Cornell’s handling of the 2024 case, which he said Cornell’s board would announce next week. He acknowledged the university does not have all the answers and must “do better” to prevent future sexual violence in the community.
DA declined additional evidence: The Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office in November 2024 declined to review any additional evidence, including more interviews gathered by the campus police department beyond the six-page statement signed by accuser Jane Doe, records obtained by the New York Times show.
fullText:
As outrage builds around the case involving a Cornell University student allegedly gang-raped in a fraternity house in October 2024, the university’s president has broken his silence with a statement Saturday.

Jane Doe’s alleged experiences raise “heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization, and aspects of party culture, alcohol, and drug use,” Kotlikoff said in his video statement.

The Cornell president added the allegations raise questions around the initial investigation, saying the university does not have “all the answers” but is committed to investigating and finding them. He said next week, Cornell’s board of trustees will announce an independent review into the handling of the 2024 case by an outside law firm.

While Cornell had released a statement after Doe filed her lawsuit in September and later launched an FAQ page on the allegations, Saturday’s remarks from Kotlikoff mark his first on-camera statement on the case.

Kotlikoff said he backs legislative efforts to change New York’s sexual assault law and Hochul’s decision to appoint a special prosecutor in the investigation – a move the university previously told CNN it supported.

While the criminal investigation and review are underway, the university will work to strengthen programs surrounding sexual assault prevention and education, mental health and substance use, he added.

Addressing frustrations surrounding Cornell’s communications about the case, he said “we will make a greater effort to explain what we can, to provide context about the actions Cornell has taken, and to be more transparent” within the confines of legal and policy limits.

Toward the end of his statement, Kotlikoff signaled support for reviewing the role of Greek organizations in campus life. “We will reengage students, alumni, and other members of our community to examine how we preserve what is valuable about Greek life while strengthening individual accountability, transparency, and a culture in which every member understands their responsibility to protect the safety and well-being of others,” he said.

Doe’s attorney, Thomas Giuffra, said he is hopeful but wary about the promises Kotlikoff made. “We are hopeful that his statement is backed up by meaningful reforms that leads to real change for the sake of the students at Cornell,” he told CNN in a statement Saturday.

Snapchat messages, a Cornell disciplinary panel’s decision, a cache of documents from the university’s formal Title IX investigation obtained by The New York Times and phone recordings by Jane Doe reviewed by ABC News have shed new light on what may have happened in the fraternity house. The sources also help clarify Doe’s reported frame of mind at points on the night that began October 19, 2024, and how her understanding of the events changed as she processed her trauma in the following weeks.

When Doe first went to campus police, authorities documented that she reported “she was recently raped by 8-10 men at the Chi Phi fraternity house,” according to documents reviewed by ABC News. CNN has asked campus police for a copy of the report.

The phrase does not appear in the six-page statement sent to prosecutors.

Cornell is facing scrutiny because the university initially said campus police investigated the allegations in 2024 and “shared all investigatory information with the Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office.” But the school later changed its statement, now saying police investigated the allegations in 2024 and “shared the victim’s sworn statement and the Snapchat screenshot” with the DA’s office.

Van Houten previously said his office did not bring criminal charges because of Doe’s six-page statement. He later said his office had access to some Snapchat messages exchanged during the alleged assault in a group chat titled, “Chi Phi Actives.” Images of one Snapchat chain obtained by CNN include a photo of Doe in a room at the fraternity house during the time she describes being assaulted.

Doe also made an explicit allegation of rape in her interview that was not included in the six-page statement furnished to prosecutors, according to WCBS. Although Doe did recount being hit and feeling emotionally coerced in the statement, it did not include some stronger language or allegations she used in her interview, according to The New York Times, citing documents it obtained.

Among the documents obtained by the Times also were records showing the district attorney’s office declined to review any additional evidence gathered by the campus police department beyond the six-page statement signed by Doe. A Cornell police investigator spoke to a member of the district attorney’s staff on November 25, 2024, about reviewing additional evidence, the Times said. By that time, university police had conducted more interviews and reviewed chat messages, the Times report said.

But prosecutors did not express interest in the additional evidence because they had decided that, based on Doe’s statement, “Criminal charges would not be pursued in this case,” a Cornell police investigator said in a note documenting the call. When reached for comment, the district attorney staff member referred all questions to the district attorney, the Times reported.

Van Houten told the Times by email that any additional records gathered by the Cornell police were “not pertinent to our analysis because we had Jane Doe’s comprehensive account of the events.” CNN reached out to Van Houten’s office for comment Friday.

CNN obtained a copy of a heavily redacted, 99-page document summarizing key evidence included in a Cornell disciplinary panel’s decision, which supports the Times’ findings about how Doe later came to understand the night’s events as assault. The panel’s decision details more than 50 interviews, including with six of the seven accused men.

Additionally, Jane Doe three weeks after the incident asked the fraternity member who invited her to the house that night, “Do you remember how any of these guys walked in?” her phone recordings reviewed by ABC News indicate.

He made no mention of his group chat invitation, ABC News reported, instead explaining to Doe, “The door was just unlocked. … The party was sort of like crowded. … There was nowhere else to go.”

Doe told him, “If I wanted to take this somewhere, what y’all did would be classified as gang rape,” she told him, ABC News reported, noting Doe’s recorded phone calls to at least three of the fraternity brothers were later turned over to university investigators.

One of the men Doe has accused of sexual assault reportedly sent her this text message: “I just wanted to apologize for how things went down the other night,” according to records obtained by The New York Times and corroborated by Doe’s attorney. The sender said he and another male allegedly involved felt terrible and too under the influence of drugs and alcohol to “shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand.”

“I’m so sorry,” another alleged attacker told Doe around the same time in a message ABC News reviewed. “I feel so bad for you, dude.”

The initial university investigation led to suspensions and expulsions for the accused students, according to Doe’s attorney, the barring of the fraternity chapter from campus and the launch of a sexual assault task force. Four of the Chi Phi fraternity members acknowledged having sexual contact with Doe but said their interactions had been consensual. The others denied participating in sexual encounters, the Times reported.

Amid the renewed investigation, court documents show a Chi Phi fraternity member named as a defendant in Doe’s civil suit has been petitioning New York state courts to invalidate a university disciplinary decision that found him responsible for attempted sexual exploitation.

Help is available: For help in the US, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673 or chat 24/7 on online.rainn.org.

CNN’s Rebekah Riess, Holly Yan, Jessie Yeung, Gloria Pazmino, Jason Carroll, Alisha Ebrahimji, Jake Tapper and Mark Morales contributed to this report.

description: Defending MotoGP champion Marc Marquez wins a sprint-race double at the Japanese Grand Prix to cut Jorge Martin's championship lead to two points.
fullText:
Reigning MotoGP champion Marc Marquez took maximum points at the Japanese Grand Prix, winning Saturday's sprint and Sunday's race, to cut fellow Spaniard Jorge Martin's championship lead to just two points.

Martin, 28, who won the title in 2024, finished second after starting Sunday's race at Motegi Circuit in pole position, while his Aprilla team-mate Marco Bezzecchi was third.

Ducati rider Marquez, 33, had to bide his time after Martin held his advantage off the line, but the seven-time champion took his chance on the 11th lap to edge past his rival on the inside.

"The race was tough, especially when I was behind Jorge, but I knew that if I was able to lead the race, my pace was good," said Marquez, who moved to 331 points with six rounds remaining.

"Jorge tried to attack, but then I just increased a bit more the pace and it was enough to do the last two laps more relaxed."

Italian Bezzecchi, 27, moved to 284 points to keep his slim title hopes alive after fending off a late charge by Tech3's Enea Bastianini to claim his place on the podium.

Gresini's Alex Marquez had a race to forget, crashing out after serving a double long lap penalty for his role in a three-rider collision during Saturday's sprint.

title: Burgess ready to stay on to end Warrington pain
description: Sam Burgess says he plans to stay at Warrington for 2027 as the Wolves try to bounce back from more Grand Final heartache.
fullText:
Warrington Wolves head coach Sam Burgess confirmed he is going to stay with the club for next year as the dust settles on yet another near miss in the Grand Final.

Saturday's 23-10 loss to Wakefield Trinity means Warrington have been losing finalists five times on Super League's biggest stage.

But having led the Wolves back to Old Trafford for the first time since 2018, Burgess - whose side also suffered narrow Challenge Cup final defeats in 2024 and 2025 - wants the pain to drive them on.

The 37-year-old is yet to agree terms for 2027 and beyond, but he has offered reassurances to the club's owner Simon Moran about his future.

"I've not signed a contract yet but I've given my word to Simon Moran and that's probably better than any contract," said Burgess.

"I truly believe in where we're going as a club and the identity we've created. In the middle of the season, we had 15 players injured and the academy system held us together.

"It'll be the same again next year and I truly believe in our philosophy."

Wakefield beat Warrington to win Super League

That philosophy was characterised by the appearances of scrum-half Ewan Irwin and centre Arron Lindop at Old Trafford.

Irwin is still only 18 and Lindop just two years older - but they contributed all 10 of their side's points against Wakefield with Lindop crossing for both tries and Irwin adding a conversion.

It is the emergence of that duo and others who are waiting in the wings that gives Burgess belief there will not be another eight-year wait to return to the domestic game's biggest stage.

"This is more of a beginning," said the man who won the National Rugby League Premiership in Australia with South Sydney Rabbitohs in 2014.

"We've understood what it takes to get here now - well certainly I have - and the squad we are building now is getting more towards 'my' squad.

"We've understood as a club and a staff what it takes to get here and we're determined to take that next step, but we have got to keep improving.

"I guess we have to let the pain of today drive us forward tomorrow."

For now, that leaves Warrington as the nearly men of rugby league with Wakefield, and not the Wire, becoming the sixth club to join the elite band of Super League winners.

title: 'New queen' Silva beats Wang to UFC flyweight title
description: Natalia Silva is crowned the new women's flyweight champion with a unanimous decision victory over China's Wang Cong at UFC 332.
fullText:
Natalia Silva was crowned the new women's UFC flyweight champion as she claimed the vacant title with a unanimous decision victory over China's Wang Cong at UFC 332.

Silva had been set to face Kyrgyzstan's Valentina Shevchenko for the title before their bout was cancelled, with Shevchenko forced to vacate the belt last month because of injury.

But the Brazilian extended her winning streak to 15 bouts with a dominant victory against Wang over five rounds in Salt Lake City.

"I want to tell this to everyone... don't give up on anything," Silva said in her post-fight interview.

"This belt here is because God gave me the opportunity. I knew [Wang] was a tough fighter. This fight proved why she was challenging me.

"This is the beginning of Natalia Silva. I'm the new queen."

The 29-year-old, who entered the bout as favourite, led the judges' scorecards with tallies of 48-47, 48-47 and 49-46.

Shevchenko later congratulated Silva on social media and warned her not to get "too comfortable".

"Well deserved Natalia! Congratulations," Shevchenko wrote on X.

"It's my pleasure to know that UFC Champion's belt is now holding deserving martial artist - such as you are.

"But don't get too comfortable - keep it warm, I'm coming soon for my belt."

It was the first women's main event in the UFC since Mackenzie Dern beat Amanda Ribas in January 2025, while it was the first time two women headlined one of the UFC's flagship numbered events since June 2023, when Amanda Nunes defeated Irene Aldana.

Earlier, Britain's Mick Parkin lasted less than four minutes in the octagon as he was knocked out by a knee from Johnny Walker on the Brazilian's heavyweight debut.

fullText:
Captain Ben Davies says Wales will be driven by a determination to prove they can thrive in Nations League A when they face Denmark in Cardiff on Sunday.

Wales go into the game in buoyant mood after ending a six-game winless sequence by taking the scalp of Norway on Thursday.

But having registered Wales' first ever victory in the Nations League's top tier, Craig Bellamy's players are hungry for more.

"We don't want to be in a situation where you feel like you're not competing against bigger teams," said defender Davies.

"But I thought we laid a good marker down the other night [against Norway] to show that we do belong playing against these teams - it was a much better all-round performance.

title: I clawed my way to the top but need a break - Azpilicueta
description: Cesar Azpilicueta says it is time to move to "a different stage of life" following a glorious 20-year playing career, notably captaining Chelsea to several titles.
fullText:
Cesar Azpilicueta was an all-encompassing leader for Chelsea - and, now retired, he reflects on how his passion for education and attention to detail helped him build a career at the highest level.

One story sums it up. Before Chelsea's Champions League final victory in 2021, Azpilicueta could not take his customary pre-match nap and opted to study instead.

He says his work towards an MBA in business management from the Berlin School of Business and Innovation took his mind off the pressure and noise on the streets of Porto.

Later that day, he lifted the Champions League trophy after captaining Chelsea to victory against Manchester City.

Azpilicueta told BBC Sport: "When I was a kid my parents pushed me to get good grades and finish school.

"I wasn't a professional footballer until I was 17, in my last year of school. Education was always important. When Covid-19 arrived, we had more time.

"I found some courses but I didn't start because I thought it was the end of my career. It was more that I wanted to learn, improve myself and do it in another language.

"It wasn't because I thought it was my last year as a footballer, but it did help me navigate the final years of my career, become a better person and a better footballer."

Azpilicueta, 37, was speaking at Arsenal's Emirates Stadium, where he joked he did not feel "entirely comfortable", while collecting a diploma in global football sport directorship through the PFA Business School, adding to qualifications that also include a diploma from Harvard Business School.

Now retired from playing after spending last season at Sevilla, he replied "maybe" when asked whether he could become a sporting director one day, but says football has left him in need of a post-career break.

Now at a "different stage of life", he cannot even contemplate playing football with friends for fun because it would trigger his competitive instincts.

"It was time to stop playing football because, even though I could probably still play, I didn't have the energy to commit myself fully for an entire season," he reflected.

"At the moment I have another commitment, which is my family. I want to play some golf and enjoy life.

"For 20 years I was constantly travelling, playing and preparing for seasons. This summer looked completely different."

After beginning at boyhood club Osasuna, Azpilicueta joined Marseille, where he learned French. However, it was his move to Chelsea in 2012 that proved transformative.

Completing his latest course highlights Azpilicueta's thirst for knowledge and a desire for constant self-improvement.

It was something he learned at Chelsea, where he arrived as a relatively low-profile £7m signing in a dressing room full of established leaders such as John Terry, Frank Lampard and Petr Cech, alongside star names including Fernando Torres, Eden Hazard and Ashley Cole.

He explained: "I started as a right winger, moved to France, then moved to Chelsea. I wasn't a star signing. I had to find my way. Left-back, wing-back, centre-back in a back three.

"It was about consistency. I had to work hard to stay fit, adapt to different managers and different positions.

"When you arrive at Chelsea, you feel the ambition straight away. Every three days you have to win. Every game and every trophy matters.

"That culture pushed me to the maximum and, especially when I left Chelsea, I felt that I had given everything I had for the club."

Azpilicueta explained how his education away from the pitch helped him develop into a leader at Stamford Bridge.

It gave him the confidence to represent Premier League players during the Covid-19 pandemic, while also helping to organise initiatives and keep the club moving forward after owner Roman Abramovich was sanctioned following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

His defining moment came in that 2021 Champions League final victory.

There is little doubt that, having succeeded Terry and then Gary Cahill as captain, Azpilicueta ranks among Chelsea's greatest leaders. Yet he revealed that, since leaving the club in 2023, he has not returned to Stamford Bridge.

He was among dozens of players to leave after Chelsea changed ownership from Abramovich to the current American-led consortium in 2022.

"I left Chelsea, but Chelsea will always stay in my heart," he said. "I follow every game and I hope the club comes back to where it belongs.

"There are some very strong teams around and football sometimes needs a bit of time. You need connections, people playing together and understanding each other.

"At a big club like Chelsea, the demands are high. But I think that's normal. It should be demanding and ambitious because, speaking as a Chelsea fan, you always want to see the club winning trophies.

"I have confidence that [manager] Xabi [Alonso], the staff and the players will do good work. Hopefully they can bring a lot of happiness to the fans."

He has been following Chelsea's latest captain Reece James, who he believes will grow into a better leader, since over-30 players Jordan Henderson, Danny Welbeck and Emiliano Martinez joined over the summer.

When it is suggested that he might return to Stamford Bridge in some capacity to be marked by a warm reception from supporters, Azpilicueta responds modestly: "I don't know about that.

"I will come back one day. I won't be putting on my boots, though."

title: Modric 'ashamed' of Croatia's 'catastrophic night'
description: Croatia captain Luka Modric says he was "ashamed" of his side's performance on a "catastrophic night" against England.
fullText:
Croatia captain Luka Modric said he felt "ashamed" of his side's performance in Saturday's 7-0 defeat at home to England in the Nations League.

It was the first time in 20 years as an international that the AC Milan midfielder said he had felt such emotion, describing it as a "catastrophic night".

Modric, 41, was making his 205th appearance for his country after recently agreeing to extend his international career under returning manager Slaven Bilic.

"You can't play football like that... we looked like we had four or five players less," said the former Real Madrid player, who helped Croatia to second-place and third-place finishes at the 2018 and 2022 World Cups during a storied career.

"It is difficult to find an explanation for such a performance without duels, fouls, aggressiveness, togetherness.

"I've been here for 20 years, but for the first time I feel ashamed after a game."

Croatia kicked off Bilic's second spell in charge with a 2-1 Nations League win away to the Czech Republic that put them above England in Group A3.

They followed that up with a chastening 4-1 defeat away to world champions Spain but were still level on points with Thomas Tuchel's Three Lions before Saturday's humiliating loss in Rijeka.

With the top two qualifying for the latter stages, Croatia had the chance to put themselves in pole position to beat England to a place in the quarter-finals.

Yet by the time Modric was substituted in the 57th minute, the home side were already 5-0 down after conceding two goals from Harry Kane and one apiece from Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Bukayo Saka.

Modric was forced to watch from the sidelines as further goals from Saka and Morgan Rogers extended England's advantage before the final whistle.

"You can lose, or play against an opponent who is better - and they are right now," added the former Spurs favourite, who helped Croatia knock England out in the qualifying stages for the 2008 Euros where they reached the quarter-finals in Bilic's first spell as manager.

"But in any case, losing like this and squandering the reputation we've built over the years is unacceptable... [it was a] catastrophic night [for Croatia]."

It does not get any easier for Croatia, who next host Spain in Split on Tuesday, and will finish their Nations League campaign with games away to England (12 November) and at home to the Czech Republic (15 November).

"We need to pull ourselves together, stay together because a new difficult game awaits us," said Modric, with Croatia third in the table, facing a battle to retain their status in the top tier of the Nations League.

"We have to show our true colours, that there is defiance and pride in us, desire, willingness, togetherness, these things cannot be lost overnight."

World number two Aryna Sabalenka followed Elena Rybakina out the door at the China Open as she fell to a surprise defeat by 34th-ranked Nikola Bartunkova.

It is the first time since 2015 that the top two seeds have failed to reach the round of 16 at the China Open.

Sabalenka has not won a title since completing the 'Sunshine Double' in March, when she triumped at Indian Wells and the Miami Open back-to-back.

It has been a mixed year for Sabalenka by her high standards. She will finish without a Grand Slam trophy for the first time since 2022 and has often struggled to control her frustrations on court.

Against Bartunkova, she failed to convert any of her five break points and she threw her racquet after falling a break down early in the second set.

title: Bowie seizing Scotland shot after World Cup disappointment
description: BBC Scotland speaks to Kieron Bowie after he scores his first goal for his country against North Macedonia.
fullText:
Sometimes, the solution to a problem can be hiding in plain sight.

On 19 May, Steve Clarke assembled his collection of players to embark on a World Cup journey.

Despite featuring and scoring for a Hellas Verona side heading for relegation from Serie A, and with a perennial problem of strikers not firing regularly for Scotland, Kieron Bowie was overlooked.

Given the loyalty Clarke showed to those who had served him so well, it was not a huge surprise. Neither was the impotence of the national team in the USA as they conjured up just one John McGinn goal.

"I received a message from him saying that I'm not in the squad but these things happen and it's just about how you bounce back from it to be honest," said Bowie.

"I scored goals in a struggling Verona team and that was as much as I could do. I was happy with where I was at and I was happy with how I'd played.

"I just spent a lot of time at home with my family and then a little golf holiday to Portugal for a week and that was all I did."

Two going on four, five or six on good night for new Scotland era

Scotland beat North Macedonia in Nations League for Pocognoli's first win

Bowie may have been cursing his luck again on Tuesday when his first international start was reduced to a mere 13 minutes following Jack Hendry's red card in the Hampden loss to Switzerland.

The landscape now looks very different.

The former Raith Rovers and Hibernian forward was one of the main Scotland heroes in Skopje after sending a deliciously whipped finish into the net in the 2-0 win over North Macedonia.

Playing in a new 3-4-1-2, Bowie started the game up top with Oli McBurnie in an ultra-attacking line up set out by Sebastien Pocognoli.

Throughout the game, his stats stacked up. The most shots with seven, the most on target with four, most shots in the box with five and the most touches in the opposition box with 11.

"You play all your life to represent a country and to score a goal is just an unbelievable feeling," said the 24-year-old Fifer.

"This manager's come in and he's put a lot of trust in me.

"I think the style that he wants to play definitely plays into my strengths. I think you've seen today a lot of times running them in behind and just showing strength against occupying defenders is one of the main things.

"It's a process but I think everyone's enjoying that process and it's a bit of a change."

The word "process" has been used so many times by the Scotland head coach and his players in recent days it's probably the new team motto.

Pocognoli is trying to implement a radically different system to his predecessor. Not only that, it's a different mindset. All while trying to embed a clutch of new players.

It's early days for the Belgian, his group, and, of course, Bowie. But the man on loan at Sassuolo believes things are clicking, and it's an opportunity for him to make his mark.

"It's a lot longer international break," he explained. "We spend a lot more time together so it's good for him to get his message across and his ideas. Also, we play more games so we have to train a little bit less of course.

"I think for me it's a fresh start with a new coach and different ideas.

"He said to me 'you don't need to prove yourself, just go and do what I know you can do' and I feel like I'm just doing that."

Bowie, who made his Rovers debut at 16, added: "I think people, obviously Scottish fans, have the same idea of how I was when I was at Hibs and that's all they can remember.

"But I feel like since I moved to Serie A, it's a different challenge against more experienced players and at a higher level.

"So, yeah, I feel like I've definitely kicked into another gear and I feel like I'm showing that."

title: Harvard beats Colgate 20-17 on a game-winning Hail Mary that included a lateral for the touchdown
description: If you're not going to make it into the end zone, you might as well make sure that you toss the ball to someone who can try to score.
fullText:
If you're going to catch a Hail Mary short of the end zone and have no way of making it across the goal line, you might as well lateral it to someone who has a chance of scoring.

That's what Harvard tight end Teigan Pelletier did on Saturday night as the Crimson beat Colgate 20-17 on a touchdown with four seconds to go.

Pelletier caught Charlie Smith's long pass short of the end zone and was in the grasp of a Colgate defender. As it was obvious he wasn't going to get into the end zone, he pitched the ball back to wide receiver Nate Bailey, who sprinted to the left corner of the end zone.

HARVARD WINS. HARVARD WINS. HARVARD WINS.#GoCrimson pic.twitter.com/CUzAP3eBck

It was a play similar to the one that Randy Moss pulled off at the end of the first half in a game against the Denver Broncos in 2003. Moss caught a Hail Mary from Daunte Culpepper well short of the end zone and was not going to score. But he flipped the ball over his head to a streaking Moe Williams, who raced untouched into the end zone.

The win pushed Harvard to 3-0 and dropped Colgate to 4-2. The Crimson are looking to get back to the FCS playoffs for a second straight season after the Ivy League rescinded its postseason ban ahead of the 2025 season. Harvard made the playoffs last year despite losing its season finale to Yale, but lost 52-7 to Villanova in the first round of the postseason.

fullText:
Simon Edvinsson's patience with the Detroit Red Wings seems to be running out.

Sportsnet's Elliotte Friedman reported late in the evening on Saturday, Oct. 3 that Edvinsson apparently has followed in the footsteps of Dylan Larkin and wants a trade.

Edvinsson's agent, J.P. Barry, declined to comment when reached by the Free Press. Wings interim general manager Shawn Horcoff met with select Detroit reporters Friday, hours before the season opener, and reiterated that signing the restricted free agent is a priority.

"We're doing everything we can, working closely with the agents," Horcoff said. "He's a big part of the club and we'd like to get him signed, but the details of the negotiation we'll keep private out of respect for Simon and his group, and we can comment on all that when it's all said and done."

More: Fans chant 'sell the team' minutes into Detroit Red Wings opener

Edvinsson, 23, is an important player for the Wings, an anchor in their top four defense corps. The 6-foot-6, 200-plus pound blueliner, drafted at No. 6 overall in 2021, had 25 points (nine goals, 16 assists) during his second full NHL season in 2025-26.

He went to the trouble of arranging for insurance so that he could join the Wings during training camp, and while he didn't participate in scrimmages or preseason games, he practiced and skated daily. But when the exhibition season ended and he was still without a contract, Edvinsson returned to his native Sweden. Given the travel distance and the six-hour time change, that showed the sides aren't close.

"I didn't expect that," Horcoff said on Friday regarding Edvinsson's departure. "We were excited when he came over," Horcoff said. "It was encouraging. I would say that's not that common, so we were excited when he came here. Of course it's disappointing when he went back, but, he's a priority for us."

The Wings lost their season opener, 2-0, to the New York Rangers, in a game marked by fans chanting "sell the team," directing their ire at owner Chris Ilitch after a summer that began with the bombshell that Larkin wanted out after 11 years, and then continued with the team parting ways with Steve Yzerman as general manager in mid-July, and the failure to sign Edvinsson before camp.

title: OpenAI's latest features take direct aim at the app store model
description: OpenAI is building out the pieces of an alternative to the traditional app store model, turning ChatGPT into a place where software can be discovered and used by people and AI agents alike.
fullText:
The focus of OpenAI’s Dev Day on Tuesday may have been on its agentic assistants known as Dots, or its new AI models, but combined, the AI company’s announcements pointed toward a bigger plan: a disruption of the traditional app store model. Taken together, today’s announcements turn ChatGPT itself into the place where software can be discovered, launched, and used by people and agents alike.

In addition, OpenAI introduced a way for people to bring their ChatGPT identity with them, while also allowing them to use their existing AI allowance in third-party apps.

This isn’t the first time OpenAI has experimented with how apps could operate within its familiar chatbot interface, but the current vision feels more fleshed out than before.

For starters, the company is turning ChatGPT itself into a surface for launching apps. The chatbot, which the company says now has 1.2 billion weekly users, has yet to fully capitalize on its potential as a discovery mechanism for finding and using apps that work with AI.

To change that, ChatGPT will begin to make app suggestions within the flow of conversation when it recognizes that a particular app could help the user complete their task. From there, the user will be able to connect the app and begin using it directly within ChatGPT.

This is also aided by the expansion of ChatGPT’s plug-in architecture, which now supports extensions.

This allows app developers to build interactive panels where users can work with their tools while they’re chatting with ChatGPT. This essentially turns the apps and services that users would have previously used via the web or through a native desktop or mobile app into something that’s operated directly within ChatGPT.

Developers that sign on with the system can build AI-native versions of their apps through ChatGPT, the same way they would through the open web or a mobile app store. As more and more discovery happens through AI chat, it’s a distribution channel that’s hard to pass up.

Users get an incentive to use that channel too, because “Sign in with ChatGPT” will let them bring their AI allowance with them. (OpenAI has 16 launch partners on this effort, including Cognition’s Devin, Notion, Vercel, T3, OpenClaw, and Dactyl, but plans to add more soon, it says.)

In a demo at OpenAI’s Dev Day event, the company showed off how its own new meeting app could work inside ChatGPT, showing upcoming meetings from the user’s calendar. Here, the user could easily choose to use AI to take meeting notes, then receive a summary of follow-up items when the meeting wrapped.

In another example, users would work with design-focused apps like those from Figma and Adobe to work on revisions of their current project or use a particular feature that would have otherwise required a stand-alone app.

The apps can be shared with others, like work colleagues, in the lightweight websites ChatGPT now produces. From these ChatGPT sites, a user’s co-workers could sign in to the app with their own credentials and permissions, making the software experience personalized to them.

OpenAI also talked about improvements to how developers submit plug-ins for review — OpenAI’s version of Apple’s App Review process, if you will. Now, developers will be able to track their review, see what needs to be fixed, request a human review, and update their plug-in’s tools without starting their whole submission over.

The company also announced a new enterprise app marketplace where partners can market their services. At launch, there are some 30-plus partners offering their app through the OpenAI Marketplace, including Adobe, Figma, Sierra, Decagon, HubSpot, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Harvey, Legora, Palo Alto Networks, CrowdStrike, Baseten, and others. Eligible customers can apply part of their OpenAI commitment toward approved partner software, OpenAI said.

Beyond turning ChatGPT into an app discovery tool where users connect with apps directly, OpenAI’s embrace of agents is gently pushing users into a new era where they don’t have to think as much about which app to use or why, relying instead on their AI agents’ suggestions.

With the launch of its autonomous AI agents known as Dots, agents will navigate the web for you, executing the tasks that need to be done in their own cloud infrastructure. Each Dot has its own cloud computer and browser, and can also use connected apps. Compare this to the old model, where users who wanted to manage some type of project — like building a website or coordinating a meeting calendar — would have to download different apps to their computer or phone to make that happen.

Now, users will instead tell an AI agent what they want to have done, and it will simply do it for them. In some cases, the agent’s work may require access to another AI model or a particular application. But this is something the agent may bring to the user, rather than the other way around — where the user is the one to go out and seek the particular tool for the job.

As OpenAI explains, the Dots will be able to connect to its ecosystem of now over 4,000 apps.

What’s more, the Dots can be proactive, perhaps jumping in to offer help with a project or bug, or handling a task the user forgot — but all done with the user’s approval. The Dots will perform what OpenAI calls “proactive research” in the background using connected apps in a read-only mode, but users would still have control over the actions they take.

This system could give app makers another way to reach customers outside of Apple and Google’s app stores. For instance, users could OpenAI has not said, however, that these features would eliminate the need for separate third-party subscriptions or other charges.

Notably, OpenAI didn’t tease any plans on this front today, instead focusing on how it’s building the discovery, distribution, and interface pieces to counter the app store model, along with an identity layer and a mechanism for sharing a user’s existing ChatGPT AI allowance. It did not announce plans Tuesday for a billing or revenue-sharing system that’s comparable to the economic layer of traditional app stores.

title: Decoding Looped Transformers Better for Almost Free
description: Looped Transformers achieve parameter efficiency by repeatedly executing a shared block across recurrent loops. Each loop yields an intermediate representation decodable for the same next token, yet standard decoding discards earlier states. Because earlier loops embody less computation, recurrence inherently supplies aligned weak-and-strong prediction pairs without auxiliary models or external training. We introduce LoopCD, a training-free contrastive decoding framework that guides token selection by contrasting the final prediction with an earlier recurrent pass, operating either in logit space with one extra output pass (LoopCD-Logits) or in hidden-state space with zero output overhead (LoopCD-Hidden). Across four looped Transformer families, LoopCD delivers substantial, consistent gains at full recurrent depth: LoopCD-Logits raises Ouro-2.

title: Kansas Legislature's Cuts Compel Fort Hays State Uni to Close Sternberg Museum
description: Fort Hays State University, grappling with a $2.4 million state-ordered spending cut, will close the Sternberg Museum of Natural History.
fullText:
TOPEKA — Fort Hays State University president Tisa Mason says the Sternberg Museum of Natural History will close to the public in mid-December because of budget problems.

She said museum faculty and staff would remain this academic year to review collections, determine what must be retained for research and teaching, and collaborate with “appropriate organizations to ensure every specimen is handled responsibly and legally.”

“This is not a decision I make lightly,” the president said Monday. “The Sternberg Museum is woven into the identity of this university and this region.”

The Sternberg Museum contains more than three million paleontology, zoology and geology specimens documenting life and environments in the Great Plains region. The collection has roots in the early 1900s, but the museum moved in a quarter-century ago to the concrete dome-shaped building in Hays adjacent to Interstate 70.

Last week, FHSU faculty, Sternberg Museum staff and community members shared disappointment with speculation the museum could be shuttered.

“I want to be clear about what closing Sternberg is and is not. It is not the cause of our budget problem,” Mason said. “When you cut into your leanest, most efficient state university, you are not trimming excess. You are cutting into muscle.”

Mason said in a 1,500-word statement that Fort Hays State received a $2.4 million reduction in state funding during the 2026 session. In addition, the Legislature requested FHSU assess how it would slash administrative costs by 10%. The university has relied for decades on revenue from higher education programs in China, but restrictions by the state could jeopardize as much as $6 million in funding.

She said closing the museum would lower Fort Hays State expenditures by $850,000 annually. That savings would be combined with $1 million in cuts across the university to compress the known budget gap to $550,000.

The museum has proven to be financially unstable with revenue annual revenue of $470,000 and average expenditures of $1.3 million per year. Complicating the issue was the $20 million in deferred maintenance at the museum.

Mason said options for Fort Hays State were limited. Unlike some higher education institutions in Kansas, FHSU doesn’t have access to local property or sales tax revenue. No individual, foundation or government entity stepped forward to underwrite the museum’s costs.

“I am open to solutions and welcome conversations and ideas,” Mason said. “But let me be direct about what any solution requires. The university would need about $1 million in new revenue every year. Not once, but annually, in perpetuity. This is a recurring cost, and it will not be solved by a one-time gift, a single fundraiser or any single event.”

In response to the $2.4 million cut imposed by the Legislature, in addition to closure of the museum, Mason said the FHSU president’s office was reorganized and staffing reduced. The university stopped hosting the Small Business Development Center and the FHSU men’s and women’s golf programs were paused in June. A new entrepreneurship director position was frozen, she said.

Mason said questions had arisen about the potential of using student tuition revenue to backfill the museum’s budget. Increases in tuition dollars have been earmarked to keep academic programs whole, she said.

“The frustration in our community right now is real, and it is understandable,” Mason said. “However, its true source is not a disagreement about whether Sternberg belongs in our academic mission. It does. That was never in question. The real source is a funding model that has asked more of FHSU than it asks of its peers.”

During fiscal year 2025, the level of state funding per full-time equivalent student ranged from a low of $6,713 at Fort Hays State to a high of $19,379 at Emporia State University.

Other full-time equivalent student funding levels in fiscal 2025: University of Kansas, $8,423; Wichita State University, $10,421; Pittsburg State University, $11,540; and Kansas State University, $11,664.

“We cannot absorb repeated, deep legislative reductions and simultaneously preserve everything our community values. Those are choices with real consequences, and those consequences fall first on the people who had no part in making them,” Mason said.

title: What is the true reach of a human being?
description: Your body stays the same size, but tools, marks, virtual worlds and AI let more of you take form beyond it. A film and reading companion on what the evidence shows, where it stops, and four questions to ask before you extend yourself.
fullText:
A narration-only film that travels from a hand stencil at least 67,800 years old to a 2025 model that turned text prompts into worlds you could move through.

We choose glasses, borrow a gesture from someone we admire, arrange a room until it feels like ours. Something inward takes an outward form, and then we live inside it.

Spectacles show how quickly a tool becomes part of a self. In a Florence sermon from early 1306 by modern reckoning, the friar Giordano da Pisa said the art of making them was not yet twenty years old. They began as a way to see. At a mirror today, the question is also: is this me?

“In time, we begin to inhabit what we have made.”

Research: the 1306 sermonReflection: living inside what we make

Tools are older than we are: flaked stones from Lomekwi 3, in northern Kenya, are about 3.3 million years old, far older than our species. Here are four later stops from the film, each paired with what the evidence does not say.

How claims are markedResearchReflectionSpeculationImagined

LIANG METANDUNO · MUNA, SULAWESI · AT LEAST 67,800 YEARS

Someone pressed a hand to the rock and sprayed pigment around it. The outline stayed. Later, its fingers were deliberately narrowed into a claw-like shape. What that meant remains open.

The date is a minimum, not a moment of creation. Calcite that formed over the stencil dates to about 71,600 years, give or take 3,800, so the stencil is at least 67,800 years old. Its maker is unknown. A trace keeps the outline of a hand, not the life behind it.

ResearchReflection: the last line

After macaques learned to rake in objects out of reach, neurons that responded to touch on the hand and to sights near it began responding along the rake. After people used a mechanical grabber, their free-hand movements and localization of touches changed, consistent with a longer represented arm.

These are changes in how the brain represents the body for a task, not physical growth. The monkey recordings came during tool use and the human measures after it; this note makes no claim about how long the effect lasts. Neither study is evidence about AI minds.

From 1363, English goldsmiths had to strike a mark of their own on their wares. An object could now carry its maker into rooms the maker would never enter.

The rule required a mark that identified the maker. Reading it as “and answers for it” is the film’s interpretation. It is also the useful part: the further work travels without us, the more it needs a name that can be found.

ResearchReflection: answerability

KALOBEYEI · TURKANA, KENYA · DESIGNED C. 2017 · FIRST SPACE BUILT 2018

Refugees and host community members learned design skills in Minecraft in workshops with UN-Habitat and the Block by Block Foundation, then planned shared public spaces. The plan provided for shade, solar lighting and more than 500 trees. Women had major roles in building the space and planting.

Software did not build the place. People did, with partners including UNHCR, the Turkana County Government and AAR Japan. In December 2018, UN-Habitat reported one of four spaces and a transport hub built, with the other three due to start in 2019.

Each time, intention travels further from the body. Each time, someone still has to choose it, build it, sign it and look after it.

The film suggests AI may widen this radius, perhaps exponentially: an idea becoming a working system, an imagined place becoming somewhere others can enter. That part is speculation. Two dated results give it texture, not proof.

Speculation: “perhaps exponentially”

METR measured a software task’s length by how long it takes a human professional. The length of tasks frontier AI agents could complete about half the time had doubled roughly every seven months over the previous six years. The report put Claude 3.7 Sonnet at about an hour.

Not a forecast, and not a measure of today’s systems, their speed or their intelligence. The authors name real-world transfer among their main uncertainties.

Genie 3 generated environments from text that a user could move through in real time, at 24 frames per second and 720p, staying consistent for a few minutes.

A limited research preview, with a limited action space, short interactions and imperfect real-world accuracy. The harbor in the film is a drawing, not model footage.

The film pictures a teacher describing a tide pool to an AI system, then shaping it with students into a small world they can explore: tap a crab, raise the tide, see what survives. Contrast it with Kalobeyei, which really happened and was built by people on the ground.

Two boundaries keep this honest. A doubling trend on particular tasks is not a law of nature. And the body-map research above concerns rakes and grabbers. It does not show that AI systems have minds, or that software becomes part of your body.

Making more is not the same as meaning more. As ideas become working systems more easily, the scarce part shifts away from making and toward the crafts the film calls old:

Reflection: the film’s argument, not a finding

Use this before you hand a task to an agent, publish a tool, or open a space to other people. There is no score. The value is in writing honest answers somewhere you will see them again.

Imagined exampleAn agent that drafts replies to customer emails.

Which part of my intention, effort or presence should travel further?

ExampleFast, consistent first drafts, so people hear back sooner.

What stays in my own hands, voice or attention?

ExampleRefunds, apologies, and anything that turns on a relationship.

Who meets this when I am not there, and who inherits it later?

ExampleA customer who gets a confident wrong answer. Whoever maintains the agent next year.

What will I check, and how often, after the excitement fades?

ExampleRead a sample of sent replies every Friday. Review everything it escalates.

This worksheet does not save or send what you type.

If your honest answer to question three is “many people,” it may be worth stepping back to the larger system before choosing the next tool. Private consulting helps clarify that system, where attention belongs, and where your next move has leverage ↗

KEEP THE REACH. BUILD THE DEPTH.

Move from interesting ideas to a repeatable practice: AI workflows, research methods, markets and attention.

Bring your questions to the Sunday conversation. Explore changing ideas and their implications through live discussion and replays.

Step back from the tools. Clarify the larger system, what deserves your attention, and where your next move has leverage.

title: AI can clone your indie game, but not its soul
description: AI can clone your indie game, but not its soul
fullText:
And that’s really the most important part! The reports of the death of building in public are greatly exaggerated.

There's no getting around the fact that agentic AI is good at operating in all modalities required to make a video game. I’m sure you’ve seen some of those posts: people are using AI to generate an entire game, based on a few reference images and specifying the mechanics in text. For example, @Stefan_3D_AI's World of Warcraft clone.

Here's another example by @JacobEisner4: this time of Minecraft. The prompt (provided in the replies) is very concise.

You can pick these apart as slop (in many cases they are), but this is the worst these models will be at this behavior, and we should be careful not to move the slopposits as they crush benchmark after benchmark. Models simply didn't have this capability even six months ago; we should all be able to admit that.

Recently, I've seen numerous accounts urging people to block an individual, @AdamHoltererer. His crime: instructing state-of-the-art AI models to clone interesting-looking demos of indie games, and posting the videos online. Adam states that he is doing this to benchmark new models like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. His detractors say he is guilty of theft.

I'm not going to get into the ethics of Adam's posts (I think there is a tendency to overreact to him, but he is capable of defending himself), however I will acknowledge I fully understand why indie developers and gamers are taking offense to this. Devs spend a long time refining games to the point where they’re ready to show them on X; and here comes some 18-year-old, purportedly copying their work with a single AI prompt. It’s a scary world to live in! Again, this is the worst these models will ever be at copying games.

Just a couple days ago, another user, @WeaselPit, recently claimed he received an from a blackmailer. The person claimed to have fully cloned his game unless he coughed up $200.

What this alleged malicious actor is doing would be illegal, and it would quickly be taken down. But with a few texture changes, it's not unreasonable to there is some way you could pull this off legally, leading many to believe you should stop “building in public.” Keep your game secret or else some vibecoder will steal your concept and beat you to the Steam release. But even if this is possible, how likely is it to happen?

Let me emphasize that the demos on X display a real capability, but what they measure is narrower than the alarmists would have you think. The model is cloning what it sees. Basic movement, visual style, some obvious mechanics. This is a surface level, shallow clone. Cloning an entire game means the entire system. The writing, the environment, the lore. The sound and the music. Solving game- or immersion-breaking edge cases. In short, how the game feels to play.

Not to mention, in order for someone to steal your game, they would have to QA it, market it, build community hype, post it somewhere, and provide post-launch support... the list goes on (as devs are painfully aware). Take a step back and think about the cool demos you've seen on X, especially the ones being cloned, and think about the effort it would really require to productionize it. Even the original devs struggle with that; and he's the one who had all the context that brought the original demo! Making a game is hard and requires artistic effort, and a bit of "magic" to be appealing to players. The "slop thief" who comes across your game will have only ever have a subset of the "magic" of your game.

Some will see this argument and say, "how do you explain what happened with 'Needle in a Haystack?'" Does this prove slop theft is already happening (albeit on a micro scale), and we can expect this to scale up to more games?

In case you aren't aware of this incident, a creator demoed his game on X and some people saw their opportunity to take his game idea and put out their own pages to capitalize off the hype. Now, there are several clones of this game on Steam and it's hard to tell who the original creator was. Kind of like finding a... well, you know.

This is kind of analogous to the mockbuster phenomenon. Low-budget studios would hear about the upcoming release of the next big Pixar movie, and capitalize off of the existing marketing (in this case, organic viral marketing). They then release a movie with similar-looking characters and art (often before the real movie!), in the hopes of duping little Timmy's grandma as she roots through the Walmart bargain bin before the new movie comes out. Now, I'm not saying a videogame "slopbuster" strategy would be completely ineffective, but my point is Ratatouille (released June 27th, 2007) wasn't ultimately overshadowed by the mockbuster Ratatoing (released June 26th, 2007), so neither will the original Needle-In-Haystack game.

Additionally, "Needle In A Haystack" is not exactly on the level of a Pixar movie. There is really not a whole lot of complexity to the idea or execution, so there is fundamentally less to clone, meaning it's more likely you could steal this concept successfully. Most people are not making a game this simple (although, perhaps they should).

So, you might tighten the claim and say, "well, maybe large games are safe, but small games are vulnerable!" Well, then this example is self-refuting. Even this game, the prototypical example of "AI cloning is real," has 23,000 playtesters alone. None of the "slop clones" come even remotely close.

One wonders if these slopbuster devs would have better luck just producing their own viral hit!

I’ve made the case that AI cloning games makes little financial sense, and is unlikely to go beyond those “benchmark” tech demos you see on X. Even knowing that, why does it still make us feel uncomfortable?

This may be discomfort about AI, generally, dressed up as discomfort for stealing games, specifically. The fact is, we live in a world where you can create something in one prompt that use to take hundreds of hours just a couple years ago. Sure, we've been tending that direction for some time (I re-made Tetris for a pre-college assignment in 2016), but this is a quantum leap. Things are changing so fast, and it's easy to despair.

There's too much to address than this one article can get into, but I'll say this: My firmly-held belief that human art intrinsically has value is why I think AI has great potential to help indie devs. It's easier than ever for an artistic, but less technically skilled, game dev to get in the game and tell their story, and that seems like a good thing to me. Just like YouTube helped people like Kane Parsons and Curry Barker hone their skills and to release high-quality art, AI will help the next generation of human artists get their foot in the door.

So, keep honing your craft. And don't be afraid to show it to the world!

title: Chalkboard and Avatar for AI Agents
description: A chalkboard and an avatar for any terminal agent: it shows its plan, its progress and its questions while it works. - zohayrslileh/more-space
fullText:
A chalkboard and an avatar for any terminal agent.
It shows its plan, its progress and its questions while it works.

More Space is a desktop app with a real terminal floating over an endless chalkboard. Run any agent in
that terminal (Claude Code, Codex, or anything else that can run shell commands) and it finds a command
there that lets it:

The command exists only inside the app's terminals and talks only to the window that opened them.
Nothing is installed in your system, and nothing is written into your project.

Builds are not signed yet. The first time:

Everything starts from the command with no arguments; each level explains the next, and
more-space --all lists everything at once. more-space guide explains the board in one screen.

Several commands can go in one call, one per line: more-space - <<'EOF' … EOF in a Unix shell,
or @' … '@ | more-space - in PowerShell.
Every write answers with the cells it really covers, and warns when it lands on something else.

The avatar also lives along by itself:

Some tools keep one background process alive and run commands through it: tmux, screen, or Codex's
shared app-server. That process keeps the environment of the terminal it was first started from.
If it was started outside More Space, it cannot see the command: restart it once from a More Space
terminal (for Codex: codex app-server daemon restart, or run codex --no-daemon). Started from any
More Space terminal, it keeps working afterwards, even across windows and restarts: the command
lives in a fixed folder and finds the window open on the project it runs in.

Boards are kept per project folder in the app's own data folder (on macOS,
~/Library/Application Support/more-space/boards/), never in the project. Pinned images are copied
there. Nothing leaves your computer, except an image the agent pins from a URL, which the app downloads.

macOS, Windows and Linux. The terminal runs your login shell on macOS and Linux, and PowerShell on
Windows (PowerShell 7 when installed, otherwise Windows PowerShell). Git must be installed for the
branch in the title and for the avatar's reactions to file changes.

The project name is defined once, in package.json; the window title, the command, the socket
variable, the data folder and the packaged app's name all derive from it.

See CONTRIBUTING.md for how to work on it, and how releases are made.

title: Great Question (YC W21) Is Hiring Product Engineers in Canada (Remote)
description: About Great...
fullText:
Great Question is the all-in-one AI customer research platform for understanding your customers. Our platform enables teams to recruit participants, run research, and share insights – all in one place. Backed by world-class investors and trusted by industry-leading teams like Gusto, Experian, Canva, and Brex, we’re building the future of customer research.

We believe AI is a multiplier for creativity, speed, and scale. Everyone on the team is encouraged to lean into AI, not just to be more efficient, but to push boundaries and unlock new possibilities. Whether you’re writing, designing, coding, or analyzing, we expect you to explore how AI can elevate your craft.

Our culture is built on high trust, high agency, and high emotional intelligence. If you’re looking for a place where your voice matters, where work is fun, and where you're empowered to do your best - join us in redefining user research 🚀

I’m PJ, CTO at Great Question. My co-founder Ned and I built this company on a simple idea: talking to your customers should be easy. This has only become more relevant as it’s become faster to build, but validating your ideas is still slow and painful.

Research, design, and product teams at ServiceNow, Brex and Canva run their customer research on us, and we raised a $13M Series A led by Inovia late last year after going through YC in 2021.

This year we’ve been doubling down on the agentic future of research. We’re super excited about what we’ve built and now we need help to continue rebuilding core parts of our product, agent-first. I’m hiring our first Product Engineers in Canada to do it with us.

Product Engineer here means you take a problem and run with it end to end - from the customer conversation to production to validating whether it actually worked. PM support is light and as-required: a PM helps size the problem, shape the appetite, and call priority, but nobody hands you a spec. From there you're trusted to find the right solution, because you're close to the customer and you have great product sense. That only works with people who are self-directed and genuinely value autonomy and accountability.

You'll build across the product stack - from Rails APIs and React/TypeScript frontends to video streaming, realtime voice agents, agentic search, product analytics, and everything in between - working directly with the founders, our designer, and the rest of engineering.

How you work. AI is embedded across your entire workflow - not just used for coding. You might spend a morning digging through interview transcripts and product analytics to understand a problem, build a few throwaway prototypes to see which approach holds up, and then build a technical plan before handing it to a couple of agents to build and QA.

We’re expecting great judgment around all of that: breaking work into sensible pieces, evaluating the output carefully, and most importantly, owning whatever ships, regardless of who typed it.

What you build. You build highly usable, customer-centric products that people love. You take the extra time to really dig into the data to make sure you understand the problem; and validate that what you’ve built actually solves it. You’ll go the extra mile to deliver something with UI + UX polish, while also thinking in systems to make sure that you’re using the right primitives so you’re delivering less bespoke solutions.

Who you are. We're a small team of exceptional engineers, and we only hire people who raise the bar.

Strong across the full stack. An expert in both exposing APIs and the frontend it sits upon. We’re a Rails and TypeScript team, but it’s not a hard requirement.

Built and run production systems. Shipping features live and then maintaining them long enough to see what works (and what doesn’t!)

Live in an agentic coding harness daily (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor - we don't care which) and have real opinions about your setup.

Ideally shipped LLM-powered features, or least know what it takes to run them in production.

Have shipped things where you decided what to build, and can defend your UX opinions.

Write clearly. We're remote and async-heavy; people who write clearly think (and prompt) clearly.

Main goes to production and approvals aren’t always required. Fast, automated CI is the gate, and we trust people to make the right judgements. Good work goes live as soon as it’s finished.

We invest in making the codebase easy to work in: written runbooks and conventions that help agents and new people find their way around quickly.

Running a few agents in parallel is easy, and expected. Sandboxes and preview environments are trivial to spawn.

You'll always have the latest tools and models, and we're generous with tokens.

Light on ceremony, high on accountability and communication.

This might not be for everyone, but if it excites you, please apply. We’re especially keen to meet people who are willing to challenge some of these ideas with their own hard-won lessons from the arena.

We expect you to hit the ground running, and fast.

Week 1: use the harness to learn the codebase and merge your first PR, ideally on day one. You’re deep in the customer data, in their Slack channels, and solving problems.

Ambiguity and shifting priorities wear you down. Problems arrive here half-shaped, and the roadmap has changed under our feet more than once this year. Some people find that energizing; if you don't, you'll hate it.

You wait to be unblocked. We’re a small team, remote, and with light processes… resourcefulness is critical to the job. We need people who unblock themselves.

You’re not all-in on AI. Dabbling won't cut it here. Agents are how we work, not a thing we're trying out.

You'd rather not talk to customers. Product engineers here get on calls, read transcripts, and sit in the support queue sometimes. That closeness is the whole point of the role.

You only want the shiny work. Plenty of weeks are polish, reliability, and making something 5% less annoying.

You want a PM to frame the problem and hand you a spec. “Just tell me what to build and I’ll build it” will not fly here.

title: Bellingham unlocks new level and potential to be 'one of the greatest'
description: Jude Bellingham's international future was being called into question a year ago, but now he is regarded as potentially one of England's "greatest of all time".
fullText:
Just a year ago, Jude Bellingham's place in the England squad was up in the air. Now he is being talked about as having the potential to be one of football's "greatest of all time".

The Real Madrid man was left out of Thomas Tuchel's Three Lions squad in October 2025 and his place at the World Cup was called into question, with the German head coach saying Bellingham wouldn't get star treatment.

But Bellingham did of course make the squad for the World Cup and was arguably his team's standout performer, finishing as England's top scorer with seven goals as they reached the semi-finals and finished third.

He has already shown that he is world class with starring performances for club and country, but the way he helped England to dismantle Croatia 7-0 in the Nations League on Saturday looked like someone perhaps reaching a new level.

The 23-year-old was instrumental in Rijeka, scoring as well as registering a hat-trick of assists. He even ended the match wearing the captain's armband as England inflicted the heaviest defeat in Croatia's history.

"Bellingham can go on to be one of the greatest players of all time," former Manchester United and Republic of Ireland midfielder Roy Keane said on ITV after the game.

"At this moment in time, he is an amazing footballer. The package – his running power, his delivery, his goal threat. The way he is progressing as a player, I still think there is a lot more to come from him."

Bellingham, recently voted England's player of the year for the second year in a row, is now "nailed on as the 10" for the future, former England defender Matt Upson told BBC Radio 5 Live.

Keane added: "He has been fantastic in possession, but what he does out of possession lifts all these other players.

"If you have a player that good in your team, who is amazing in possession and he's playing for Real Madrid and doing brilliant things, but his work rate off the ball... that will just inspire other players. He is a huge leader for them."

England's front four will share praise for the way in which they demolished the Croatian backline.

Record goalscorer Harry Kane scored twice, as did Bukayo Saka, with Anthony Gordon scoring and assisting too.

And Kane will be back in the spotlight on Tuesday when he can equal Peter Shilton's all-time England men's appearance record against the Czech Republic at Wembley.

In moving to 89 goals for his country, the 33-year-old again showed how irreplaceable he is for England, but, when he was rested with 20 minutes to go, it was Bellingham who took the captain's armband.

And that highlighted the younger man's importance as a leader within the squad.

Bellingham was also directly involved in more than two goals in an England game for the first time, and he became the first player to record three assists in a game for the Three Lions since Trent Alexander-Arnold against San Marino in November 2021.

It was Bellingham's performance in front of goal that impressed former England striker Ian Wright.

"When Bellingham is on the pitch, he is always driving forward and going again and again," Wright said.

"He was involved in everything. His athleticism, his technical ability, his intensity. He never lets up, the way he gets in the box, he is always in there unmarked. He is always in there."

Bellingham showed every aspect of his game against Croatia and Tuchel was asked by BBC Sport if he had gone to another level.

"Yes, at the moment it seems like it, and you always need to," Tuchel said.

"It's like you can never stand still. You have to develop and you have to push for the next level, otherwise other teams will catch up."

Tuchel, who said the performance was a way to "move on" after the disappointment of England's World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina, said that he "adjusted some things" following the tournament, giving players, including Bellingham, "a lot of responsibility".

Saka was part of the front four and Bellingham assisted his first goal with a high quality cross.

"He was amazing tonight," Saka said of Bellingham.

"He deserved player of the year and he deserved man of the match tonight too. He was special.

"[I'm] happy to play with him and happy to have him in the England team."

title: Whittaker survives late scare to hold on for points win
description: British light-heavyweight Ben Whittaker survives a dramatic late onslaught from Conor Wallace to move a step closer to a world-title shot with a points victory in Birmingham.
fullText:
British light-heavyweight Ben Whittaker survived a dramatic late onslaught from Conor Wallace to move a step closer to a world-title shot with a points victory in Birmingham.

The 29-year-old controlled much of the contest with his trademark showboating and superior boxing skill at the Utilita Arena before Wallace came roaring back in the championship rounds.

The Northern Irishman rocked Whittaker in the 10th and came close to a remarkable turnaround in the 12th, with the home fighter forced to hold on until the final bell.

The judges scored it 117-111, 116-112 and 115-113 as Whittaker became mandatory challenger for the IBF world title.

"It was too easy and I took my eye off the ball a little bit. He caught me with a good shot but that's boxing," Whittaker said.

"When it got a bit too easy I was playing too much and doing silly antics."

The Olympic silver medallist extended his unbeaten professional record to 13 wins and one draw and is now mandatory challenger for IBF champion Dmitry Bivol, who also holds the WBA 'super' and WBO belts and is expected to face Liverpool's Callum Smith in December.

Wallace, 30, suffered the second defeat of his 19-fight career and called for an immediate rematch.

"If he wants to run it back and get a beat down again he can. If not, we'll move on," Whittaker responded.

Whittaker made an extravagant entrance, accompanied by a live string ensemble playing WWE star The Undertaker's theme before switching to "Icon" by Karen.

Despite being from nearby West Bromwich, Whittaker was greeted by as many jeers as cheers from the roughly 5,000 fans inside the arena.

The fight came alive in the third when Whittaker briefly staggered Wallace with a shot that skimmed his forehead.

Wallace's travelling support made themselves heard, only to be drowned out by an airhorn smuggled into the arena as Whittaker found his rhythm

Among those in attendance were former UFC champion Leon Edwards and American Cassondra Gainey, who travelled nearly 4,000 miles from North Carolina after Whittaker's social-media videos helped lift her spirits during cancer treatment.

Wallace offered a warning of what was to come when he landed a heavy left in the sixth.

"Stay focused. Just because you're comfortable, don't get lazy," trainer Andy Lee told Whittaker, who regained control before an almost disastrous 10th round.

Wallace hurt him with a thudding southpaw left before Whittaker walked on to a huge shot and looked in serious trouble.

Whittaker briefly got some respite when Wallace was warned for punching on the break, but he continued pushing forward as a major upset suddenly felt possible.

Whittaker hit the canvas three times in the final round, none ruled knockdowns, as Wallace threw everything at a visibly tiring opponent.

"I only have myself to blame," he said. "I feel like I've got the best support in the world. This felt like my home show tonight even though it's in Birmingham."

Promoter Eddie Hearn welcomed the possibility of a rematch: "We know Ben is in the position to fight the winner of Bivol-Smith but it's likely that won't be until next summer, so he needs to fight in the interim."

On a strong undercard showcasing domestic talent, there was British-title success for Walsall's Hamza Uddin and Londoner Bilal Fawaz.

Nigeria-born Fawaz, who is fighting for a British passport, stopped Eithan James in the eighth round to retain his British and Commonwealth light-middleweight titles.

Fawaz – who earned a £5,000 stoppage bonus offered to him by promoter Hearn earlier in the night - called out IBF world champion Josh Kelly and Conor Benn after his win.

"It doesn't matter who is in front of me, with the capacity of what we are trying to achieve, no one can stop us except if they are at world level," Fawaz told BBC Radio 5 Live.

Unbeaten Uddin, 23, dominated Sean Bruce, dropping him twice in the fifth with punishing body and head shots for an eighth straight win.

Uddin closed the show in the eighth with a heavy right. Bruce rose at the count of nine before the referee stepped in.

Given star billing in the chief support on his professional debut, standout amateur Odel Kamara, 22, dominated Thodoris Ritzakis, dropping the Greek in the first before a somewhat premature third-round stoppage.

"Liverpool has a star. Britain has got a star. This kid is going all the way," Hearn said of the debutant.
